scenario: Today's generative recommendation track asks whether the objective and the list structure catch up after a model starts generating the next item directly. Reinforcement learning can lift clicks and revenue, but it can also turn the model into a better ranker and a worse retriever, with candidate recall falling on all five datasets studied. Some work replaces a scalar reward with verbalized feedback, some writes query evidence into identifier learning and decoding, and some uses hyperbolic geometry or full-sequence diffusion to settle codebook hierarchy and the entire page of results. Large-model sequential recommenders start to keep long histories and multiple interests together, and raise pass-through rate online; collaborative graph supervision can be written into training without becoming inference cost. A shopping-agent evaluation adds a caution: longer thinking raises stated confidence without necessarily choosing better products.

papers.title: Stable and Granular Policy Optimization for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Muyu Zou, Haibo Xing, Hao Deng, Zhezheng Hao, Jinxin Hu, Jiawei Chen, Yun Chen, Yu Zhang, Xiaoyi Zeng
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation (GR), which directly generates sequential semantic IDs for items, has recently attracted increasing attention in recommender systems. Given that core recommendation metrics are inherently evaluated at the sequence level, reinforcement learning (RL) serves as a natural optimization framework. However, adapting recent group-based RL algorithms to GR presents notable challenges: token-level methods such as GRPO exhibit much more severe training instability, while sequence-level methods such as GSPO enforce uniform token weighting and thus ignore the heterogeneous roles of tokens. To address this dilemma, we propose Stable and Granular Policy Optimization (SGPO), a group-based RL algorithm tailored for GR. SGPO maintains a sequence-level ratio to promote optimization stability while injecting fine-grained token-wise advantages.  By incorporating token log-probabilities and reward signs, SGPO explicitly upweights high-confidence tokens in positive trajectories to reinforce successful retrieval, while strictly penalizing them in negative trajectories to encourage exploration, and uses an adaptive scaling factor to bound the variance of reshaped advantages. Experiments on two public benchmarks and a billion-scale industrial dataset show that SGPO consistently outperforms six strong RL baselines and, when deployed on a commercial platform, achieves a 2.36% lift in click-through rate (CTR) and a 1.95% increase in advertising revenue in online A/B testing.
papers.summary: Generative recommenders decode sequential semantic IDs for items, and because core metrics are scored at the sequence level, reinforcement learning is a natural fit. Off-the-shelf group-based algorithms struggle here: token-level methods become much more unstable, while sequence-level methods weight every token equally and ignore their different roles. A group-based method built for this setting keeps a sequence-level ratio for stability while injecting token-wise advantages. It upweights high-confidence tokens on positive trajectories to reinforce successful retrieval, strictly penalizes them on negative ones to encourage exploration, and uses an adaptive scale to bound the variance of the reshaped advantages. On two public benchmarks and a billion-scale industrial dataset, it consistently beats six strong reinforcement-learning baselines. In an online test on a commercial platform, click-through rate rose 2.36% and advertising revenue rose 1.95%.

papers.title: Better Rankers, Worse Retrievers: The Hidden Cost of RL Post-Training in Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Yuheng Chen, Fan Zhang, Yixuan Xu, Chao Yang, Yang Xiang, Can Yang
papers.abstract: Generative recommenders decode the semantic ID of a user's next item with a language model, and post-training them with reinforcement learning (RL) after supervised fine-tuning (SFT) has become standard practice. The gains are mostly reported on the first ten results, yet in deployment such models hand hundreds of candidates to a downstream ranker or reward model. We show that RL post-training has a hidden cost: it improves accuracy at the top of the list (hit@K for small K) but, on all five datasets we study, lowers the recall of the candidate list (hit@K for K in the hundreds). The model becomes a better ranker and a worse retriever. Controlled experiments trace the loss to the negative advantages that RL assigns to the candidates it samples, the rollout. The root cause is that only one next item is logged per user, so RL treats every other candidate as wrong. Yet these candidates are the model's most plausible alternatives, and often the next items of other users with similar histories. Penalising them pushes down exactly what similar users choose next, and these items drop out of those users' candidate lists. This diagnosis points directly to a remedy: out-of-rollout anchoring, a single additional loss term that preserves the SFT model's ordering of the items outside the rollout. It keeps the gain at the top and restores recall to the SFT level on all five datasets, and it is effective under other RL configurations as well. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic study of this recall loss: we measure it, identify its cause, and show that, once the cause is known, a simple remedy suffices.
papers.summary: Post-training generative recommenders with reinforcement learning after supervised fine-tuning is now standard, but gains are usually reported on the first ten results, while deployed models often hand hundreds of candidates to a downstream ranker. A systematic measurement shows that reinforcement learning improves accuracy at the very top, yet on all five datasets studied it lowers recall of the candidate list: the model becomes a better ranker and a worse retriever. The cause is that only one next item is logged per user, so the most plausible alternatives in the rollout are treated as wrong and given negative advantages, and items that similar users would choose next drop out of those lists. An out-of-rollout anchoring term that preserves the supervised model's ordering of items outside the rollout keeps the gain at the top and restores recall to the supervised level on all five datasets. On Office, hit@500 falls from 52.84% to 47.69%, which shows how large this hidden cost can be.

papers.title: HyMiRec: A Hybrid Multi-interest Learning Framework for LLM-based Sequential Recommendation
papers.authors: Jingyi Zhou, Cheng Chen, Kai Zuo, Manjie Xu, Zhendong Fu
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated strong potential for sequential recommendation. However, current LLM-based approaches face critical limitations in modeling users' long-term and diverse interests. First, due to inference latency and feature fetching bandwidth constraints, existing methods typically truncate user behavior sequences to include only the most recent interactions, resulting in the loss of valuable long-range preference signals. Second, most current methods rely on next-item prediction with a single predicted embedding, overlooking the multifaceted nature of user interests and limiting recommendation diversity. To address these challenges, we propose HyMiRec, a hybrid multi-interest sequential recommendation framework, which leverages a lightweight recommender to extracts coarse interest embeddings from long user sequences and an LLM-based recommender to captures refined interest embeddings. To alleviate the overhead of fetching features, we introduce a residual codebook based on cosine similarity, enabling efficient compression and reuse of user history embeddings. To model the diverse preferences of users, we design a disentangled multi-interest learning module, which leverages multiple interest queries to learn disentangles multiple interest signals adaptively, allowing the model to capture different facets of user intent. Extensive experiments are conducted on both benchmark datasets and a collected industrial dataset, demonstrating our effectiveness over existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, online A/B testing shows that HyMiRec brings consistent improvements in real-world recommendation systems.

retrieval_meta.raw_source_name: Proceedings of the ACM Web Conference 2026

papers.summary: When large models are used for sequential recommendation, latency and feature-bandwidth limits often force the system to truncate behavior sequences to recent interactions, dropping long-range preferences; predicting a single embedding also struggles to cover a user's many interests. A hybrid multi-interest framework uses a lightweight recommender to extract coarse interests from long sequences and a large-model recommender to refine them, and a residual codebook based on cosine similarity compresses and reuses history embeddings to cut feature-fetch cost. A disentangled multi-interest module uses multiple queries to learn different facets of intent. On public benchmarks and industrial data it improves over existing large-model methods, with an average gain of 24.53% on PixelRec and 8.9% on MovieLens-1M. In an online test, pass-through rate on image-and-text traffic rose from 26.46% to 30.93%, showing that long sequences and multiple interests can fit an online budget.

papers.title: More Than What Was Chosen: LLM-based Explainable Recommendation Beyond Noisy User Preferences
papers.authors: Chung Park, Hyeongjun Yun, Taesan Kim, Junui Hong, Dongjoon Hong, Mira Myong, Jihoon Oh, MinCheol Cho, Kijung Park, Min sung Choi, Jihwan Seok, Jaegul Choo
papers.abstract:
Recommender systems traditionally rely on the principle of Revealed Preference (RP), which assumes that observed user behaviors faithfully reflect underlying interests.
While effective at scale, this assumption is fragile in practice, as real-world choices are often noisy and inconsistent.
Thus, even LLM-based recommendation models (LLM-Rec) equipped with advanced reasoning capabilities may fail to capture genuine user preferences and often produce rationales of limited persuasiveness.
To address this issue, we introduce the concept of Coherent Preference (CP), which complements RP by favoring items that are logically and causally coherent with user interaction history.
Building on this perspective, we propose Conflict-Aware Direct Preference Optimization (C-APO), an LLM-Rec framework that jointly optimizes RP and CP while adaptively reconciling their agreement and conflict, delivering robust recommendation performance and logically consistent rationales. 
We construct a unified ordering approach that combines the RP signal, based on chosen versus unobserved items, with the CP signal, which ranks items by their logical consistency with past interaction history.
In this unified preference ordering, we dynamically adjust the influence of each signal depending on whether RP and CP agree or conflict, allowing the model to better capture user intent and generate more plausible recommendations.
On the Amazon Review dataset, our approach consistently outperforms approximately 20 state-of-the-art baseline models in both recommendation performance and rationale quality, achieving a 1.65$\times$ relative improvement in click-through rate during deployment, thereby demonstrating its practical utility.
The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/cpark88/C-APO.
papers.summary: Recommenders usually assume that observed choices faithfully reflect underlying interests, but real-world choices are often noisy and inconsistent, so even large-model recommenders with reasoning may miss genuine preferences and produce unconvincing rationales. One approach complements revealed preference with a coherent-preference signal that favors items logically and causally consistent with interaction history, and jointly optimizes both in a unified ranking. The influence of each signal is adjusted depending on whether the two agree or conflict, so the model can learn from chosen items without being tied to a single noisy click. On Amazon review data, the method consistently outperforms about 20 strong baselines in both recommendation performance and rationale quality, and it achieved a 1.65 times relative improvement in click-through rate after deployment. For teams that want large models to recommend and explain, ==clicked items should not be treated as the whole of user interest.==

papers.title: IntentGR: Enhancing Intent for End-to-End Personalized Generative Retrieval in Search
papers.authors: Gefan Ye, Yanjing Wu, Yinfu Feng, Zhiqiang Wang, Liang Li, Jun Xiao, Rong Xiao, Xiaoyi Zeng
papers.abstract: Personalized generative retrieval in search should jointly satisfy the user's immediate search intent and long-term preference. Recent end-to-end approaches, primarily explored in recommendation, unify item tokenization and sequence generation within a single model, allowing semantic identifiers (SIDs) to be optimized toward the downstream generation objective. However, these methods often treat the query merely as an input feature, without explicitly leveraging it to guide either identifier learning or sequence generation. This leaves intent guidance weak in both the tokenization and the generation stage, causing generated semantic identifiers to drift toward high-frequency token patterns rather than the current search intent. In this work, we find that incorporating additional query-related evidence into the framework of end-to-end generative retrieval is important. Based on this finding, we propose IntentGR, an intent-enhanced end-to-end framework that strengthens query semantics at four complementary stages of the retrieval pipeline. Query-Aware Semantic Behavior Representation (QBR) introduces query-level behavioral evidence as a new input signal; Query-Semantic Alignment (QSA), Long-Tail Query Enrichment (LQE), and Query-conditioned Attention Modulation (QAM) then serve as integration mechanisms at the optimization, training-distribution, and decoding stages to fully exploit this evidence. Experiments on the public AOL4PS benchmark and AE, a large-scale industrial e-commerce dataset, show that IntentGR improves Recall@10 by 8.11% and 11.96% over the strongest baseline, with strong gains on long-tail queries. These results suggest that enriched query-related input evidence, together with effective integration mechanisms, is beneficial for building intent-aware end-to-end generative search systems.
papers.summary: Personalized generative retrieval in search needs to satisfy both the current query intent and longer-term preference. Existing end-to-end methods often treat the query as just another input feature, without using it to guide identifier learning or sequence generation, so the generated semantic IDs drift toward frequent token patterns rather than what the query is looking for. An intent-enhanced framework adds query-related evidence at four stages of the retrieval pipeline: it brings in query-level behavioral evidence as a new input, then applies semantic alignment, long-tail query enrichment, and query-conditioned attention at the optimization, training-distribution, and decoding stages. On the public AOL4PS benchmark and a large-scale industrial e-commerce dataset, it raises Recall@10 by 8.11% and 11.96% over the strongest baseline, with especially clear gains on long-tail queries. The implication is that ==end-to-end generative search should write query evidence into identifier learning and decoding==, rather than treating the query as a mere prefix.

papers.title: Hyperbolic RQ-VAE enhanced Generative Recommendation with Differential-Length Codebook Strategy
papers.authors: Aoran Zhang, Yu-Bin Yang, Yonghong Yu
papers.abstract: Recently, the integration of large language models (LLMs) with generative recommendation (GR) has demonstrated promising potential. However, most existing GR methods adopt residual quantization to implicitly model hierarchical relationships across codebook layers in Euclidean space, which distorts the intrinsic tree-like hierarchy and leads to low codebook utilization. To address these issues, we propose a Hyperbolic RQ-VAE enhanced Generative Recommendation, namely HG-Rec. Specifically, HG-Rec enhances the residual quantization mechanism by embedding the latent discrete representations into hyperbolic space to explicitly model hierarchical relationships across codebook layers. Motivated by the exponential volume growth of hyperbolic space, we further design a differential-length codebook strategy, i.e. the codebook size follows a pyramidal structure, which aligns with the tree-like structure and effectively compresses the codebook size. Hence, benefiting from the alignment of hyperbolic geometry and codebook hierarchy, HG-Rec achieves lower collision rates, more uniform codebook usage, and less training time compared to existing methods. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that HG-Rec consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance. The code is available in the https://github.com/zar123123/HG-Rec.
papers.summary: When large models are joined with generative recommendation, most methods still run residual quantization in Euclidean space and only implicitly model hierarchy across codebook layers, which can distort a tree-like structure and leave codebook utilization low. A hyperbolic residual-quantization method embeds the discrete latent representations in hyperbolic space to model that hierarchy explicitly. Motivated by the exponential volume growth of hyperbolic space, it also uses a pyramidal, differential-length codebook, which aligns with the tree structure and compresses codebook size. After the geometry and the codebook hierarchy are aligned, collision rates are lower, codebook usage is more uniform, and training takes less time than existing methods. Across multiple benchmarks, the approach consistently reaches the strongest reported generative-recommendation results. For teams that assign semantic IDs to items, ==hierarchy is worth expressing directly in the geometry==, not only approximating it layer by layer with residuals.

papers.title: More Than a Score: Reinforcement Learning with Verbalized Feedback for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Zipeng Chen, Xinyu Lin, Yuliang Sun, Sheng Zhang, Zeyu Wang, Xiaowen Shi, Junwei Pan, Chengguo Yin
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for generative recommendation, where recommended items are generated directly from users' interaction histories. To further improve recommendation quality, reinforcement learning (RL) has been applied to align these models with recommendation objectives. However, existing RL methods rely on scalar rewards to implicitly guide exploration. These rewards do not specify which aspects of a candidate conflict with the user's preferences or how the next candidate should differ. To address this gap, we propose VerRec, a verbalized feedback-guided RL framework for generative recommendation. Specifically, a user simulator generates personalized verbalized feedback based on the user's historical preferences and the candidate item profile. The policy uses this feedback to produce refined recommendations. Original and refined candidates form an expanded group and are jointly optimized with group relative policy optimization. The user simulator is only required during training and is removed at inference time. Experiments on three Amazon review datasets with two generative recommendation backbones demonstrate that VerRec improves recommendation accuracy and ranking quality. Further analyses show that verbalized guidance encourages exploration of more diverse candidates and helps the policy discover more rewarding recommendations during training.
papers.summary: Generative recommenders are increasingly aligned with recommendation objectives through reinforcement learning, but most methods use only a scalar reward, which does not say which aspects of a candidate conflict with a user's preferences or how the next candidate should differ. A verbalized-feedback framework lets a user simulator write personalized comments from the user's history and the candidate profile. The policy then produces refined recommendations, and the original and refined candidates form an expanded group that is optimized together with group-relative policy optimization. The simulator is used only in training and is removed at inference. On three Amazon review categories and two generative backbones, the method significantly improves hit rate and ranking quality; on Cell Phones, hit@20 rises from 0.0671 for the strongest baseline to 0.0730. Analyses also show that verbalized guidance encourages more diverse candidates and helps the policy find more rewarding recommendations during training.

papers.title: Full-Sequence Masked Diffusion for Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract:
Autoregressive large language models have dominated generative recommendation by sequentially predicting the next item. However, this unidirectional paradigm suffers from error propagation, and limited ability to jointly optimize an entire recommendation list.
In this paper, we introduce Full-Sequence Masked Diffusion for generative recommendation (FSMD), which extends masked diffusion models to enable global joint modeling over the entire user history and Top-$K$ recommendation list. We formulate recommendation as a unified sequence diffusion process, where the forward process randomly masks tokens across the full sequence and the reverse process simultaneously denoises all masked positions using bidirectional context.
This formulation enables parallel generation of the entire recommendation list and naturally captures inter-item dependencies within a coherent global structure. To better align generation with ranking objectives, we further introduce a unified training objective that combines masked diffusion likelihood with a listwise ranking loss.
Extensive experiments on multiple public benchmarks demonstrate that FSMD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art autoregressive and item-level diffusion-based generative recommendation methods across accuracy and list quality metrics.
papers.summary: Autoregressive large models have dominated generative recommendation by predicting the next item in order, but this one-way generation propagates earlier errors and has a limited ability to optimize an entire recommendation list jointly. A full-sequence masked diffusion method treats user history and the top recommendations as one diffusion process: the forward pass randomly masks tokens across the full sequence, and the reverse pass denoises every masked position at once with bidirectional context. The entire list can therefore be generated in parallel, and dependencies among items are captured inside a coherent global structure. To align generation with ranking, training combines a masked-diffusion likelihood with a listwise ranking loss. On multiple public benchmarks, the method consistently outperforms the strongest autoregressive and item-level diffusion generative recommenders on both accuracy and list quality. For systems that must return a whole page of recommendations, ==items on the list should be generated and scored together==, not guessed one after another.

papers.title: R-GRec: Relation-Guided Generative Recommendation via Collaborative Graph Supervision
papers.authors: Xiangfu Meng, Jiapeng Yang, Lei Shi, Xue Wang, Yuefeng Zhan, Chen Gu, Hao Sun, Weiwei Deng, Tao Yao, Feng Sun, Qi Zhang
papers.abstract:
Generative recommendation has recently emerged as a promising paradigm for large-scale recommendation by reformulating next-item prediction as discrete sequence generation. However, current SID-based models rely mainly on history-to-next-item supervision, leaving item--item collaborative topology only indirectly captured through sparse user sequences. To address this gap, we propose *R-GRec*,  a graph-derived structural supervision framework for SID-based generative recommendation. From user interactions, *R-GRec* builds an item--item graph and derives three complementary auxiliary objectives---Neighbor Prediction, Topological Contrast, and Link Prediction --- to make collaborative topology explicit during generative training.

Extensive experiments on the two public Amazon datasets demonstrate that R-GRec achieves state-of-the-art performance over representative traditional, generative, and LLM-based recommenders. Further ablation and analytical studies verify the contribution of each graph-derived objective and show that collaborative topology acts as a complementary supervision signal to Semantic ID generation, improving generative recommendation without adding inference-time graph computation.
papers.summary: Semantic-ID generative recommenders mostly learn from history-to-next-item supervision, so item-item collaborative topology is only captured indirectly through sparse user sequences. A relation-guided framework builds an item-item graph from interactions and adds three complementary auxiliary objectives: neighbor prediction, topological contrast, and link prediction, so collaborative structure is supervised explicitly during generative training. On two public Amazon datasets, the method outperforms representative traditional, generative, and large-model recommenders. Ablations show that each graph-derived objective contributes, that collaborative topology is complementary supervision for semantic-ID generation, and that no graph computation is added at inference time. For teams adopting generative recommendation, ==item-item collaboration can be written into training== without becoming extra cost at serving time.

papers.title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.
papers.summary: Large models are increasingly used as autonomous shopping agents that read multimodal product listings and recommend purchases, and it is natural to assume that thinking harder will yield better choices. A benchmark of ten frontier models on three product-choice suites built from WebShop, Amazon SQID, and Wayfair WANDS tests that belief. Across all three benchmarks, raising thinking effort does not improve decision quality in a statistically meaningful way, but it does raise stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. Most models are also poorly calibrated at every effort level. Errors are strongly shared: when several models all err on a task, more than 80% of them pick the same most popular wrong product. For anyone deploying shopping agents, ==a longer thinking trace is not a guarantee of better product choices.==
